candidates.title: AOMEI Backupper update servers tampered with to push a downloader and backdoor

discovery.usageRights: Citation and short paraphrase only; check publisher terms before reuse.

candidates.dedupeCheck: No seed incident or candidate mentions AOMEI.

claims.statement: Attackers repeatedly tampered with files AOMEI Backupper fetched from the vendor's update servers between April and July 2026 to distribute a backdoor, without exploiting a software vulnerability.

ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab, working with Google GTIG and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign; ManageEngine first flagged AOMEI Backupper installing Radmin at two unrelated companies on May 28 and notified AOMEI on June 7.
Attackers briefly modified two update and notification config files and changed the expected checksum so the malicious archive passed verification; the files were restored within minutes.
Payloads included a previously unknown downloader (CROSSROAD) and a backdoor (SHINYROAD) that abuses legitimate Radmin components; on July 20 Google observed an attempt to steal Windows NTLM hashes.
Named affected organizations were in the US, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain and Switzerland across IT services, telecom and higher education; no total victim count was given.
AOMEI initially suggested in-transit interception, which ManageEngine disputed; AOMEI later said it patched its servers and has not confirmed how attackers got in.

unresolvedQuestions: Primary source found (ManageEngine report); claims still cite BleepingComputer and SC World, which match it on the May 28 detection and the UNC7017, CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD names.
Cause is disputed between AOMEI (possible interception, no breach found initially) and ManageEngine (altered on AOMEI's side).
Attribution to UNC7017 is from reporting; do not add actor links per the ATT&CK rules.
Credential angle limited to an NTLM hash theft attempt; no secrets exposure reported.

claims.statement: Trojanized DAEMON Tools Lite installers signed with the developer's certificates were distributed from the official website; versions 12.5.0.2421 to 12.5.0.2434 were affected starting April 8, 2026.
Three binaries were trojanized (DTHelper.exe, DiscSoftBusServiceLite.exe, DTShellHlp.exe), with a backdoor that runs whenever they launch and can download and run executables on command.
Kaspersky saw several thousand infection attempts in more than 100 countries and territories; further-stage payloads reached only about a dozen machines, suggesting targeted intent.
The vendor released clean version 12.6.0.2445; the developer said unauthorized interference in its build environment caused the compromised packages.
Researchers noted Chinese-language strings in the collector but did not attribute the compromise to a specific actor.

unresolvedQuestions: Exposure window started April 8, before the six-month window of this batch; included because it ran into May 2026.
Vendor confirmation is via news coverage; the vendor's own statement was not fetched.
No credential or secrets theft reported; payloads were a collector, backdoor and RAT.

claims.statement: On June 1, 2026, at least 32 packages under the @redhat-cloud-services npm namespace were compromised; the malicious versions averaged about 80,000 combined weekly downloads.
A compromised Red Hat employee GitHub account pushed malicious orphan commits to RedHatInsights repositories, bypassing code review; workflows then published packages with valid SLSA provenance.

The payload, Miasma, derives from the Mini Shai-Hulud source released publicly in May and targets GitHub and npm tokens, SSH keys, AWS/GCP/Azure credentials, Kubernetes tokens, Vault secrets and CI/CD secrets.
Unit 42 says attribution is uncertain because the public Mini Shai-Hulud source lets other actors copy the attack.

unresolvedQuestions: Primary source needed: no Red Hat statement or original discoverer write-up was fetched.
Unit 42 describes what the payload targets; confirmed theft from specific victims is not reported.

candidates.dedupeCheck: No seed incident or candidate covers the June 3-4 binding.gyp wave; distinct from incident:redhat-cloud-services-npm-miasma-2026 (June 1) though the payload family overlaps.

claims.statement: Over a 10-hour window on June 3-4, 2026, an attacker published 286 malicious versions of 56 npm packages, including 24 autotel-* packages, without using a lifecycle hook.
The attacker added binding.gyp to pure JavaScript packages so npm's node-gyp step silently ran a loader during install.

The payload checked more than 30 CI-related environment variables and collected AWS, Azure, GCP and GitHub Actions credentials plus local files such as ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, SSH keys, .npmrc and .env, then committed them to attacker-controlled GitHub repos.
It could republish trojanized packages with stolen tokens, inject hooks into AI coding assistant configs, and run a destructive dead-man's switch if its GitHub token was revoked.
Sonatype tracked the wave as 281 malicious package versions that abuse binding.gyp and steal credentials and self-propagate.
StepSecurity counted 57 packages across more than 286 malicious versions in a rolling campaign lasting under two hours.
Chainguard reported @vapi-ai/server-sdk at about 408,000 monthly downloads and ai-sdk-ollama at about 120,000 among the affected packages.

unresolvedQuestions: Counts differ by source: ReversingLabs 56 packages / 286 versions; Sonatype 281 versions; StepSecurity 57 packages / 286+ versions.
How the npm publish tokens were obtained is not established by ReversingLabs.
Reviewer decides whether this and the Red Hat incident should be one campaign record.

claims.statement: Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a compromise of the @asyncapi npm organization on July 14, 2026; five package versions were republished within about ninety minutes.

A pull_request_target workflow ran attacker-controlled PR code, exposing the asyncapi-bot token; legitimate release workflows then published the packages with valid provenance. Microsoft says its records do not establish how the credential was obtained.
Affected versions were @asyncapi/specs 6.11.2-alpha.1 and 6.11.2, @asyncapi/generator 3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-components 0.7.1 and @asyncapi/generator-helpers 1.1.1.
The payload runs at import time, so --ignore-scripts does not stop it; it loads the Miasma runtime for C2, remote access and persistence on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Credential-harvesting modules for npm, AWS, GitHub and cloud tokens were present but disabled in the analyzed build; Microsoft still recommends rotating credentials from a clean host.
Unit 42 calls the campaign miasma-train-p1 and says the payload descends from the Miasma RAT used in the June Red Hat operation, with different initial access.

unresolvedQuestions: No confirmed credential theft in the analyzed build; modules could be enabled later.
Number of affected organizations not quantified.

claims.statement: Netskope Threat Labs analyzed 28 malicious npm package versions published on 2026-08-04 across four unrelated enterprise namespaces: @servicetitan, @or-sdk, @onereach and @umacloud.
The package's CI/CD collection paths pay off on build agents, but it also runs on developer machines and the operator collects from both.
The exfiltration endpoint domain was resolved at runtime from Ethereum contract state, so Netskope treats it as perishable.

claims.statement: Checkmarx researchers found indexed-btree impersonating the legitimate sorted-btree library; it reached nearly 2 million weekly downloads before removal on September 3, 2026, about 11 weeks after the first malicious version.
The malicious code sat in the runtime method BTree.prototype.set rather than an install script, launching an obfuscated loader when called with a specific key.
The loader fingerprints the host and exfiltrates via Slack and Telegram; its C2 address is stored in a Sepolia Ethereum testnet smart contract.
The campaign bypasses the npm security measures GitHub announced in June 2026 by avoiding installation scripts, and can delete its files and remove the trigger code.

unresolvedQuestions: Checkmarx's write-up confirms the BTree.prototype.set trigger, Slack and Telegram exfiltration, the Sepolia contract and file self-deletion, but gives no removal date; the September 3 date and 11-week figure come from CSO Online.
No credential theft reported; the second-stage payload is undescribed.
Download figures for a typosquat may include automated installs; treat as reported, not as victims.

claims.statement: Ten malicious releases of @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen, a package with about 150,000 weekly downloads, were published on August 28, 2026 across every maintained version line.
Socket analysts identified the activity as an ongoing Mini Shai-Hulud compromise.

The install-time payload, triggered via binding.gyp and in some releases a pre-install command, searched project files, process memory, cloud metadata and CI variables for tokens, validated them, and stored encrypted results in attacker-created public GitHub repos.
StepSecurity reproduced the installation behavior under Harden-Runner and warned not to install the latest version.

unresolvedQuestions: Socket's write-up confirms ten malicious versions with valid provenance; Cyber Security News reports a release workflow that a pull request comment could trigger, letting attackers publish fork code. Confirm the workflow detail from Socket before promotion.
Earlier chat summary dated this October 11; the source says August 28, 2026, with the article published September 1.
